Hailie · England housing waiting lists

Households on the housing register: trends and forecasts, 1987–2025

A consolidated analysis of MHCLG Live Table 600 — the national and regional trend, a leakage-free rolling-origin backtest of seven forecasting models, and what they do (and don't) tell us about 2026–2030.

Source: MHCLG Live Table 600, retrieved 7 Aug 2026 · Report generated 17 August 2026

  2. 1. The national and regional trend

Executive summary

1,340,527 households on the register, 2025
+17.9% change since 2020 (1,137,234 → 1,340,527)
ETS damped trend best 1-year model · 4.09% MAPE
Naive best 5-year model · 22.10% MAPE

The England total is not a trend — it traces two full cycles since 1987, falling to a trough of 1,020,229 in 1998, rising to a peak of 1,851,884 in 2012, falling again to a shallower trough around 2018, and rising since 2020 to 1,340,527 in 2025. Seven benchmark forecasting models were compared with leakage-free rolling-origin backtesting. No single model wins at every horizon: a damped-trend exponential smoother (ets_damped) is most accurate one to two years out, but the simplest possible model — carry the last value forward (naive) — is hardest to beat from three years out onward, because every trend-following model eventually overshoots when the cycle turns.

1. The national and regional trend

England's housing register total is not monotonic. Over 1988–2025 (38 year-on-year changes), 21 years saw an increase and 17 a decrease — the largest single-year rise was +16.1% (2003) and the largest fall was −18.8% (2014). Register counts can move for administrative reasons (periodic list “cleanses”) as well as genuine change in housing need; this report does not attempt to separate the two (see Limitations).

Regional picture

The nine English regions sum exactly to the England total. They do not move uniformly — London and the South West show the largest proportional rise since 1987, while the North East and East Midlands show the largest falls — but every region traces the same broad rise-peak-fall-rise shape as the national series (see chart).

2. Forecasting method

Seven models were compared, all evaluated identically with rolling-origin (walk-forward) backtesting: at each origin year from 1996 to 2024, every model is trained only on data up to and including that year (an expanding window), then forecast 1/2/3/5 years ahead; the forecast is compared against the actual value once it becomes available. No model ever sees data from after its origin year — this is checked structurally in code, not just asserted in prose.

ModelIdeaDependency
NaiveLast observed value, held flatNone
DriftLast value + average historical slope × horizonNone
Linear trendOLS straight-line fit, extrapolatedNone
SESExponentially-weighted level (no trend), α grid-searchedNone
Holt's linearExponentially-weighted level + trend, α/β grid-searchedNone
ETS damped trendHolt's method with the trend damped toward flat over the horizonstatsmodels
ARIMAOrder (p,d,q) chosen per origin by AIC, restricted to well-conditioned fitsstatsmodels

A real bug was found and fixed during this work: an early, unconstrained version of the ARIMA order search picked a numerically degenerate model at one origin — its AR and MA roots sat exactly on the unit circle, producing a forecast of precisely 0.0 households. The fix rejects any candidate order whose roots come within 1.05 of the unit circle. Full diagnosis: docs/statistical_models_methodology.md §2.

3. National backtest results

Mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), lower is better, best model per horizon highlighted:

Model1-year MAPE2-year MAPE3-year MAPE5-year MAPE
ETS damped trend4.09%8.51%13.59%26.16%
ARIMA4.19%9.10%14.50%30.97%
Holt's linear4.25%9.25%14.74%31.36%
Naive4.71%9.03%13.32%22.10%
SES4.75%9.06%13.36%22.12%
Drift5.03%9.82%14.71%25.89%
Linear trend19.16%22.71%26.41%34.16%

ETS damped trend is the strongest model at 1- and 2-year horizons — it damps Holt's trend term just enough to avoid most of the overshoot that makes the undamped Holt model swing wildly around turning points, while still tracking the post-2020 upturn faster than the flat models. From the 3-year horizon on, though, the simplest model in the comparison — naive — is hardest to beat (with SES close behind it), because every trend-aware model eventually extrapolates through a cycle turn and pays for it, and that catches up with even the damped version by 3 years out. Linear trend is the weakest model at every horizon by a wide margin, for the same reason: it cannot represent a series that rises, falls, rises, falls.

4. Regional results

The same seven-model comparison was run separately for each of the nine English regions. Two findings stand out. First, every region is harder to forecast than the smoother national total (higher MAPE at every horizon) — aggregation cancels out some of each region's own noise. Second, the best model varies by region as well as by horizon:

Caution: most of naive's apparent wins above are decided by under 0.1 MAPE points against SES — effectively a tie, not a real difference (full analysis: docs/regional_forecast_methodology.md §2.4). Read the win counts as “naive/SES/ETS-damped are all competitive here,” not as one model dominating.

5. Illustrative 2026–2030 forecast

Each of the seven models was fit on the full 1987–2025 series and extrapolated forward. This is not a validated prediction — it has not itself been backtested, only the methodology that produced it has. Given the backtested MAPEs above (roughly 4–5% at 1 year, rising to 22–34% at 5 years depending on model), every row below should be read as a wide-uncertainty benchmark, not a point estimate to plan against. The highlighted cell in each column is the model with the lowest backtested MAPE at that horizon (Section 3) — so the forecast emphasised here is the one the evaluation actually supports, not a separately-chosen model. 2029 has no highlighted cell: it sits at a 4-year horizon, and the backtest only evaluates 1/2/3/5-year horizons, so there is no evaluation result to select from at that year.

6. Limitations

  • Not a complete measure of housing need. Live Table 600 counts households on local authorities' own housing registers only; it excludes housing-association-run registers where these are separate from the council list, so the true scale of social housing demand is understated to a degree that varies by area.
  • Administrative “cleanse” effects are not separated from genuine demand change. Councils periodically review and remove applicants from their registers; a fall in the reported count can reflect this rather than reduced need. This data alone cannot distinguish the two.
  • No exogenous drivers. Every model here uses only the series' own history — none accounts for policy changes, local housing supply, or economic conditions that plausibly drive some of the swings shown above.
  • Small, overlapping backtest samples at longer horizons. The 5-year backtest has 25 origins nationally, and the same 25 origins independently in each of the 9 regions — but consecutive origins share almost all of their training data, so these are not 25 independent trials — treat horizon-level MAPE as indicative of relative model performance, not a precise confidence interval.
  • Local-authority-level forecasting was not attempted. Unlike the clean regional data used here, the local-authority extract mixes pre- and post-reorganisation authority codes (boundary changes through 2019–2023) that would need reconciling first — documented but not resolved in docs/initial_feasibility_note.md §2.
  • ARIMA's automatic order search can still produce implausible long-horizon forecasts even after the unit-root fix above — including one negative forecast at a training window ending near a sharp trend change. These were reported, not clipped or hidden; see docs/statistical_models_methodology.md §4.

7. Reproducing this work

Every number and chart in this report is generated by a script, in order, from the raw MHCLG source file. Nothing is hand-edited or estimated by eye. 

python3 scripts/prepare_data.py         # raw extracts → processed long-format CSVs
python3 scripts/validate_national.py    # England-total figures vs. raw extract
.venv/bin/python3 scripts/explore_national.py    # EDA charts and headline stats
.venv/bin/python3 scripts/forecast_national.py   # national backtest, 5 base models
.venv/bin/python3 scripts/forecast_regional.py   # regional backtest, 5 base models
.venv/bin/python3 scripts/forecast_statistical.py  # + ets_damped, arima (national & regional)
python3 scripts/build_report.py         # this report

Full technical detail, QA checks, and the complete decision log for every choice above (why an expanding window, why MIN_TRAIN_YEARS=10, why these four horizons) live in docs/national_forecast_methodology.md, docs/regional_forecast_methodology.md, and docs/statistical_models_methodology.md.
